blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has published no examiners' comments for Paper 6; the guidance below comes from its suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.

**This is the highest-scoring chapter of the paper.** A cost-of-capital question has appeared in every past paper from May 2024 to May 2026, usually as a 5 to 10 mark part of Question 1 or Question 2, and in every RTP and almost every MTP.

The standard question gives a capital structure and asks for the cost of each source and then the **weighted average cost of capital** — eight of the thirty-five official questions here take exactly that form.
**CAPM is the single most tested formula** in the chapter: it opened the January 2025, January 2026 and September 2024 papers.
**Convertible debentures** are the favourite twist: you must first decide the redemption value as the higher of the cash value and the value of the shares on conversion.

blocks.title: How ICAI marks this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: Marks follow the **formula, the working note and the answer**. Each cost — Kd, Kp, Ke, Kr — is usually worth one to two marks, and the WACC table one to three.

**Present the WACC as a four-column table** — source, amount, weight, cost, product — exactly as the study material's own illustration does.

concepts.title: 1–3. Introduction, the Meaning of Cost of Capital and its Significance
understand: **Why the chapter exists (§1).** The basic task of a finance manager is **procurement of funds and their effective utilisation**, and the objective of financial management is **maximisation of the wealth of shareholders**. ==Here **wealth or value is equal to performance divided by expectations**.== The finance manager must therefore select a capital structure **in which the expectation of investors is minimum, hence shareholders' wealth is maximum** — and for that he first needs to calculate the cost of each source of finance.

**Meaning (§2).** ==**Cost of capital is the return expected by the providers of capital — shareholders, lenders and debt-holders — to the business, as compensation for their contribution to the total capital.**== When an entity procures finance it has to pay some **additional amount of money besides the principal**, either as a **one-off payment or a regular payment at specified intervals**. This additional money is the **cost of using the capital**, and **expressed as a rate it is used to discount or compound the cash flow or stream of cash flows**.

==Cost of capital is also known as the **'cut-off' rate, 'hurdle rate' or 'minimum rate of return'**.== It is used as a **benchmark for framing debt policies of an entity and for taking capital budgeting decisions**.

**Significance (§3).** The correct cost of capital helps in three decisions. **(i) Evaluation of investment options:** the estimated future cash flows from available opportunities are **converted into present value by discounting them with the relevant cost of capital**; since **every investment option may have a different cost of capital**, it is important to use the one relevant to the option. **(ii) Financing decision:** when choosing between two sources of finance, the manager can **compare their cost and choose the source which has the lower cost**, and besides cost may also consider **financial risk and control**. **(iii) Designing of optimum credit policy:** while appraising the credit period to be allowed to customers, **the cost of allowing credit is compared against the benefit or profit earned**, and cost of capital is used to arrive at **the present value of costs and benefits received**.
concepts.example: A project promising 14% is accepted if the company's cost of capital is 11% and rejected if it is 16% — the same project, two answers, because the hurdle rate changed.

concepts.title: 4. Determination of Cost of Capital — and What Moves It
understand: ==**Cost is not the amount which the company plans to pay or actually pays — rather it is the expectations of stakeholders.**== Stakeholders here include the **providers of capital** (shareholders, debenture holders, money lenders), **intermediaries** (brokers, underwriters, merchant bankers) and the **Government** (for taxes).

**The study material's own example.** If a company issues **9% coupon debentures but the expectation of investors is 10%**, investors will **subscribe at a discount and not at par**, so the **cost to the company will not be 9% but 10%**. Besides the return to investors, the company must also pay **commission, brokerage and fees to intermediaries**, which **increases the cost above 10%**. On the other hand, **payment of interest is a deductible expense under the Income-tax Act, which reduces the cost of capital to the company**.

**The cash flows to identify.** Cost of any source of finance is **expressed as a percentage per annum**. To calculate it, identify: **(1) inflow of the amount received at the beginning; (2) outflows of interest, dividend and redemption amount; (3) inflow of tax benefit on interest, or outflow of dividend tax.** Then **use the trial and error method to arrive at the rate where the present value of outflows equals the present value of inflows — that rate is basically IRR**.

==In investment decisions **IRR indicates income**, because there an initial outflow is followed by a series of inflows. In the cost of capital chapter, **this IRR represents cost**, because here an **initial inflow is followed by a series of net outflows**.==
**Alternatively, shortcut formulas may be used.** The study material's caution: **though these shortcut formulas are easy to use, they give an approximate answer and not the exact answer**.

**Factors affecting the cost of capital (§4).** **Supply and demand** — like any good, the cost of capital is influenced by supply and demand; **when there are many exciting business opportunities there is more competition for funding, driving the cost up**, and when opportunities are scarce **investors are more willing to lend at lower rates**. **Investor preferences** — cultural factors and personal savings habits affect the overall pool of available capital, and **higher potential returns generally lead to more savings**. **Risk and return** — there is always a trade-off; **high-risk ventures must offer a higher potential return**, but **if the cost of capital becomes too high it can make the project unprofitable**. **Inflation** — investors look for **returns that outpace inflation so their money retains its buying power**. **Exchange rates** — for multinational companies, **fluctuations add an extra layer of risk and affect the overall cost of capital**.
concepts.example: A 9% debenture sold at a discount to yield 10%, plus 1% issue expenses, costs the company more than 10% before tax — and less than that after the interest tax shield.

official_questions.question: Consider the following statements and state whether each is true or false: (1) a debt-equity ratio of 2:1 indicates that for every rupee of equity there are two rupees of debt; (2) the cost of floating a debt is greater than the cost of floating an equity issue.
answer_points: **Statement 1 is true.** A debt-equity ratio of 2:1 means that for every one rupee of shareholders' funds there are two rupees of outside liabilities (SM Ch 3 §3.2.1).

**Statement 2 is false.** The cost of floating a debt issue is generally **lower** than that of an equity issue, because debt carries less risk for the investor and the issue process is simpler; floatation cost is the underwriting or brokerage fees, legal and administrative charges, registration fees and printing expenses incurred to make securities available to investors (SM §5.2).
Beyond the floatation cost, the cost of debt itself is lower because **interest is a deductible expense under the Income-tax Act**, giving a tax shield that dividends do not.
official_questions.conclusion: One mark; both halves must be right.

concepts.title: 5–5.2 Cost of Long-term Debt, the Features of Debentures, and Irredeemable Debentures
understand: **What long-term debt is (§5).** External borrowings or debt instruments **do not confer ownership** on the providers of finance. The providers **do not participate in the affairs of the company but enjoy the charge on the profit before taxes**. Long-term debt includes **long-term loans from financial institutions and capital from issuing debentures or bonds**. ==The **calculation of the cost of a loan from a financial institution is similar to that of redeemable debentures**.==

**Features of debentures or bonds (§5.1).** **Face value** — the denominated value, on which interest is calculated (a 9% non-convertible debenture of ₹100 carries interest of 9% on ₹100). **Interest or coupon rate** — each debenture bears a fixed rate **except zero coupon and deep discount bonds**, payable periodically. **Maturity period** — a fixed period for redemption; **for irredeemable debentures the maturity period is not defined and is taken as infinite**. **Redemption value** — determined by the debt covenants and **may vary from the face value**. **Benefit of tax shield** — **interest paid to debenture holders is allowed as an expense for corporate tax, so it saves tax liability; that saving is known as the tax shield**.

**The study material's tax-shield illustration.** X Ltd. is fully equity financed and Y Ltd. uses debt. Both have **EBIT of ₹100 lakh**. Y Ltd. pays **interest of ₹40 lakh**, so its profit before tax is ₹60 lakh against X Ltd.'s ₹100 lakh. At **35% tax**, X Ltd. pays ₹35 lakh and Y Ltd. ₹21 lakh, giving profit after tax of ₹65 lakh and ₹39 lakh. ==The interest payment of ₹40 lakh results in a **tax shield of ₹14 lakh** (₹40 lakh × 35%), so the **effective interest is ₹26 lakh only**.==
**Two categories by redemption:** **irredeemable debts** and **redeemable debts**.

**Cost of irredeemable debentures (§5.2).** Debentures not redeemed by the issuer during the life of the company. ==**Kd = I(1 − t) ÷ NP**, where **Kd** is the cost of debt after tax, **I** the annual interest payment, **NP** the net proceeds of debentures or the current market price, and **t** the tax rate.==

==**Net proceeds means issue price less issue expenses or floatation cost.** If the **issue price is not given, assume it equals the current market price**. If **issue expenses are not given, assume them to be zero**.==

**Floatation cost.** ==A new issue of a security, debt or equity, involves expenditure in the form of **underwriting or brokerage fees, legal and administrative charges, registration fees and printing expenses**; the sum of these is the **floatation cost**, incurred **to make the securities available to the investors**, and it is **adjusted to arrive at net proceeds** for the calculation of cost of capital.==

**The study material's floatation illustration.** A company issues **1,000 15% debentures of face value ₹100 each at a discount of ₹5**, with **underwriting and other costs of ₹5,000**. It actually realises **₹90,000** — ₹1,00,000 less ₹5,000 discount and ₹5,000 underwriting expenses. The **annual interest of ₹15,000 is therefore the cost of obtaining the ₹90,000 actually received**.
concepts.example: A 12% irredeemable debenture of ₹100 issued at ₹95 with ₹2 of issue expenses has net proceeds of ₹93; at 30% tax, Kd = 12 × 0.70 ÷ 93 = 9.03%.

expected_questions.question: A company issues 1,000 15% irredeemable debentures of face value ₹100 each at a discount of ₹5. Underwriting and other costs are ₹5,000 for the total issue. The tax rate is 35%. Compute the cost of the debentures, and explain what floatation cost is.
answer_points: **Net proceeds.** The company realises ₹1,00,000 less ₹5,000 discount and ₹5,000 underwriting expenses = **₹90,000**, so net proceeds per debenture are ₹90.
**Annual interest** = 15% of ₹1,00,000 = **₹15,000**, which is the cost of obtaining the ₹90,000 actually received.

**Floatation cost** is the expenditure a new issue of a security, debt or equity, involves in the form of underwriting or brokerage fees, legal and administrative charges, registration fees and printing expenses. It is incurred to make the securities available to investors and is adjusted to arrive at net proceeds for the calculation of cost of capital.

Note that net proceeds means issue price less issue expenses; if the issue price is not given it may be assumed equal to the current market price, and if issue expenses are not given they may be assumed to be zero.

concepts.title: 5.3 Cost of Redeemable Debentures (Approximation Method)
understand: ==**Cost of Redeemable Debenture (Kd) = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2]**==, where **I** is the interest payment, **NP** the net proceeds or current market price, **RV** the redemption value of the debentures, **t** the tax rate applicable to the company and **n** the remaining life of the debentures.

That formula is used **where only interest on debt is tax deductible**. Sometimes debts are **issued at a discount and/or redeemed at a premium**. ==If the **discount on issue and/or premium on redemption are tax deductible**, the alternative formula is **Kd = {[I + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2]} × (1 − t)**.==
==**In the absence of any specific information, students may use any of the above formulae to calculate the cost of debt with a logical assumption.**==

**The study material's warning about accuracy.** These formulas give an **approximate value** of the cost of debt. ==In these formulas, **the higher the difference between RV and NP, the lower the accuracy of the answer**. One should therefore **not use these formulas if the difference between RV and NP is very high**. They are also **not suitable in case of gradual redemption of debentures or bonds**.==

**Illustration 2 of the study material.** A company issued 10,000 10% debentures of ₹100 each **at a premium of 10%** on 1.4.2023, to be **matured on 1.4.2028** and **redeemed at par**. Tax is 35%. Here **I = ₹10, NP = ₹110, RV = ₹100, n = 5 years, t = 0.35**. So Kd = [₹10(1 − 0.35) + (₹100 − ₹110) ÷ 5] ÷ [(₹100 + ₹110) ÷ 2] = (₹6.50 − ₹2) ÷ ₹105 = ₹4.50 ÷ ₹105 = **0.0428, or 4.28%**.

**Illustration 3 of the study material.** The same company issued the debentures **at par** on 1.4.2018 to mature on 1.4.2028 at par, and wants the cost of its **existing** debt on 1.4.2023 when the **market price is ₹80**. Here **I = ₹10, NP = ₹80 (the current market price), RV = ₹100, n = 5 years, t = 0.35**. So Kd = [₹10(1 − 0.35) + (₹100 − ₹80) ÷ 5] ÷ [(₹100 + ₹80) ÷ 2] = (₹6.50 + ₹4) ÷ ₹90 = ₹10.50 ÷ ₹90 = **0.1166, or 11.67%**.

Notice what the two illustrations teach between them: **a debenture issued at a premium costs less than its coupon**, and **a debenture now trading below par costs more** — because in each case it is the **net proceeds or market price, not the face value, that sits in the denominator**.

concepts.title: 5.3.1–5.3.2 Cost of Debt by the Present Value Method (Yield to Maturity), and Amortisation of a Bond
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (Sep 2024 Q2(a), May 2026 Q1(b)) · MTP 1 (Sep 2025 Series I)
understand: **The present value method (§5.3.1).** The cost of redeemable debt is also calculated by **discounting the relevant cash flows using the internal rate of return**. ==**Yield to maturity is the annual return of an investment from the current date till the maturity date; it is the internal rate of return at which the current price of a debt equals the present value of all cash flows.**==

**The relevant cash flows.** **Year 0:** net proceeds in case of a new issue, or the current market price in case of existing debt (NP or P0). **Years 1 to n:** **interest net of tax, I(1 − t)**. **Year n:** the **redemption value (RV)**.

**Three steps.** **Step 1:** identify the cash flows. **Step 2:** calculate the net present values of those cash flows **using two discount rates (guessing)**. **Step 3:** calculate the IRR by interpolation: ==**IRR = L + [NPV<sub>L</sub> ÷ (NPV<sub>L</sub> − NPV<sub>H</sub>)] × (H − L)**==.

**The study material's worked example.** 10,000 10% debentures of ₹100 each issued 1.4.2023 maturing 1.4.2028; market price ₹80; tax 35%. Cash flows: year 0 **₹80**; years 1 to 5 **₹6.50** (10% of ₹100 × 0.65); year 5 **₹100**. At 10% the NPV is **+₹6.74** and at 15% it is **−₹8.51**, so IRR = 10% + [6.74 ÷ (6.74 − (−8.51))] × (15% − 10%) = **12.21%**.

==**Yield to maturity, or the present value method, is a superior method of determining the cost of debt of a company compared with the approximation method, and it is also preferred in the field of finance.**== The same caution applies as before: **the higher the difference between H and L, the lower the accuracy of the answer**.

**Illustration 4 — the deep discount bond.** Institutional Development Bank issued **zero-interest deep discount bonds of face value ₹1,00,000 each, issued at ₹2,500 and repayable after 25 years**, with no corporate tax. Because there is a **huge difference between RV and NP, the approximation method is unsuitable and trial and error is used**: ₹1,00,000 = ₹2,500 × (1 + r)<sup>25</sup>, so **40 = (1 + r)<sup>25</sup>**. At 15%, (1.15)<sup>25</sup> = 32.919; at 16%, (1.16)<sup>25</sup> = 40.874. Interpolating, **IRR = 15.89%**.

**Amortisation of a bond (§5.3.2).** A bond may be **amortised every year, i.e. the principal is repaid every year rather than at maturity**. The **principal goes down with annual payments and interest is computed on the outstanding amount**, so **the cash flows of the bond will be uneven**. ==The value of a bond amortised every year is **V<sub>B</sub> = Σ C<sub>t</sub> ÷ (1 + Kd)<sup>t</sup>** for t = 1 to n.==

**Illustration 5.** RBML proposes to sell a **5-year bond of ₹5,000 at 8% interest per annum, amortised equally over its life**; the investor expects a minimum return of **6%**. Interest declines each year as the outstanding falls: **₹400, ₹320, ₹240, ₹160 and ₹80**. With ₹1,000 of principal returned each year, the outflows are **₹1,400, ₹1,320, ₹1,240, ₹1,160 and ₹1,080**. Discounted at 6%, these give **₹1,320.75 + ₹1,174.80 + ₹1,041.14 + ₹918.88 + ₹807.05 = ₹5,262.62**, the value of the bond.

Discount at two trial rates, compute both NPVs, and interpolate using IRR = L + [NPV<sub>L</sub> ÷ (NPV<sub>L</sub> − NPV<sub>H</sub>)] × (H − L).

**Cost of redeemable preference shares (SM §6.2).** Kp = [PD + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2] = [₹12 + (₹105 − ₹104) ÷ 5] ÷ [(₹105 + ₹104) ÷ 2] = (₹12 + ₹0.20) ÷ ₹104.50 = **0.1167, or 11.67%**. Note that there is **no (1 − t)**: preference dividend is not tax deductible.

official_questions.question: Z Ltd. has issued 8% convertible debentures of ₹100 each with a remaining maturity period of five years. The current market price per debenture and the conversion terms are given. Compute the cost of the debentures.
answer_points: **Step 1 — determine the redemption value (SM §5.4).** For a convertible debenture, the redemption value is the **higher of the cash value of the debenture and the value of the equity shares receivable on conversion**, because it is assumed that all debenture holders will choose the option with the higher value.

The value of the shares on conversion is the **number of shares per debenture × the market price grown at the historical growth rate over the remaining life**, i.e. **n shares × P0(1 + g)<sup>t</sup>**.

**Step 2 — compute the cost.** With RV fixed, apply either the approximation formula Kd = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2], or the present value method with year 0 the current market price, years 1 to 5 interest net of tax of ₹8(1 − t), and year 5 the redemption value.

ICAI's answer for this paper works the growth rate first — 8.03 = 5(1 + g)<sup>7</sup>, giving 1.606 = (1 + g)<sup>7</sup> and **g = 7%** — and then the price of the share after five years, before setting the redemption value.
The examinable step is the redemption value decision, not the division that follows.
official_questions.conclusion: Redemption value first, cost second — in that order, every time.

official_questions.question: A company issues 15% convertible debentures of ₹100 each at par with a maturity period of 6 years. On maturity the debenture holders will have the option to convert into equity shares of the company on stated terms. Compute the cost of the debentures.
answer_points: **Redemption value** = higher of (i) the cash value of the debenture, ₹100, and (ii) the value of the equity shares on conversion, being the number of shares per debenture multiplied by the market price compounded at the growth rate over six years.
**Cost by the approximation method** = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2], with I = ₹15, NP = ₹100 (issued at par), n = 6 years.
**Cost by the present value method** = the IRR of: year 0 ₹100 inflow; years 1 to 6 outflow of ₹15(1 − t); year 6 outflow of the redemption value. Interpolate between two trial rates.

The study material's own Example 3 follows exactly this structure for a 15% convertible debenture with a 5-year maturity and a 1:10 conversion ratio, reaching 16.09% by approximation and 17.43% by the present value method — a useful reminder that the two methods do not agree.
official_questions.conclusion: Both methods are acceptable; say which one you used.

concepts.title: 5.4 Cost of Convertible Debentures
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (May 2024 Q2(a), Jan 2025 Q2(a), Jan 2026 Q1(c)) · MTP 1 (May 2025 Series II)
understand: The holders of convertible debentures have the option **either to get the debentures redeemed into cash, or to get a specified number of the company's shares in lieu of cash**. The calculation is **very much similar to that of redeemable debentures**, with one decision first.

==**While determining the redemption value of the debentures, it is assumed that all the debenture holders will choose the option which has the higher value, and accordingly it will be considered to calculate the cost of debentures.**==

**The study material's Example 3.** A company issued **10,000 15% convertible debentures of ₹100 each with a maturity period of 5 years**. At maturity holders may convert into equity shares **in the ratio of 1:10 (10 shares for each debenture)**. The **current market price of the equity shares is ₹12 each** and the **historical growth rate is 5% per annum**. Tax is 35%.

**Determination of redemption value.** Higher of **(i) the cash value of the debentures = ₹100**, and **(ii) the value of the equity shares = 10 shares × ₹12(1 + 0.05)<sup>5</sup> = 10 × ₹15.312 = ₹153.12**. ==**₹153.12 is taken as the redemption value, as it is higher than the cash option and is more attractive to the investors.**==

**Cost by the present value method.** Post-tax interest per annum = ₹100 × 15% × 0.65 = **₹9.75**. Cash flows: year 0 **₹100**; years 1 to 5 **₹9.75**; year 5 **₹153.12**. At 15% the NPV is **+₹8.78** and at 20% it is **−₹9.29**, so IRR = 15% + [8.78 ÷ (8.78 − (−9.29))] × (20% − 15%) = **0.17429, or 17.43%**.
Note that the **two methods give 16.09% and 17.43%** on the same facts. Say which method you are using; ICAI accepts either unless the question directs one.

concepts.title: 6–6.2 Cost of Preference Share Capital, Irredeemable and Redeemable
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (May 2024 Q2(a), Sep 2024 Q2(a), Jan 2026 Q1(c))
understand: Preference shareholders are **paid dividend at a specified rate on the face value** of preference shares. **Payment of dividend is not mandatory but is given priority over the equity shareholder.** ==The payment of dividend to preference shareholders is **not charged as an expense but treated as an appropriation of after-tax profit**; hence **dividend paid to preference shareholders does not reduce the tax liability of the company**.== Like debentures, preference share capital can be **redeemable or irredeemable**.

**Cost of irredeemable preference shares (§6.1).** ==The cost is **similar to the calculation of a perpetuity**: **Kp = PD ÷ P0**, where **PD** is the annual preference dividend and **P0** the net proceeds from the issue of preference shares.==

**Net proceeds** again means **issue price less issue expenses or floatation cost**; if the **issue price is not given, assume it equals the current market price**, and if **issue expenses are not given, assume them to be zero**.
**Illustration 6.** XYZ Ltd. issues **2,000 10% preference shares of ₹100 each at ₹95 each**. Kp = PD ÷ P0 = (₹10 × 2,000) ÷ (₹95 × 2,000) = ₹10 ÷ ₹95 = **10.53%**.

**Cost of redeemable preference shares (§6.2).** Preference shares redeemed on maturity. The cost is **similar to the cost of redeemable debentures with the exception that the dividends paid to preference shareholders are not tax deductible**. ==**Kp = [PD + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2]**==, where **PD** is the annual preference dividend, **RV** the redemption value, **NP** the net proceeds from issue and **n** the remaining life.

The cost of redeemable preference shares **may also be calculated as the discount rate that equates the net proceeds of the sale of preference shares with the present value of the future dividends and principal payments** — the same present value method used for debt.

**Illustration 8.** XYZ Ltd. issues **2,000 10% preference shares of ₹100 each at ₹95**, proposing to redeem them **at the end of the 10th year**. Kp = [₹10 + (₹100 − ₹95) ÷ 10] ÷ [(₹100 + ₹95) ÷ 2] = (₹10 + ₹0.50) ÷ ₹97.50 = **0.1077, or 10.77% (approx.)**.
==Put the two families side by side and the whole difference is one bracket: **Kd carries (1 − t); Kp does not.**==
concepts.example: September 2024 gave preference shares redeemable after 5 years at a 5% premium, selling at ₹104: Kp = [₹12 + (₹105 − ₹104) ÷ 5] ÷ [(₹105 + ₹104) ÷ 2] = ₹12.20 ÷ ₹104.50 = 11.67%.

concepts.title: 7–7.2 Cost of Equity Share Capital: the Dividend Price and Earnings Price Approaches
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Sep 2025 Q1(a)) · MTP 2 (Mar 2024 Series I, Sep 2026 Series I)
understand: **Why there is no single formula (§7).** Just like any other source of finance, **cost of equity is the expectation of equity shareholders**. Value is performance divided by expectations; **if we know the value and the performance, we can calculate expectation as a balancing figure**. Here **performance means the amount paid by the company to investors** — interest, dividend, redemption price. ==**In the case of debentures and preference shares the amount of interest or dividend is fixed, but in the case of equity shares it is uncertain.**== Hence there is **not a single method but different methods**, depending on the facts.

**The study material's own decision rule.** **(1)** If **dividend is expected to be constant**, use the **dividend price approach**. **(2)** If **earnings per share is expected to be constant**, use the **earnings price approach**. **(3)** If **dividend and earnings are expected to grow at a constant rate**, use the **growth approach (Gordon's model)**. **(4)** If it is **difficult to forecast future dividend or EPS**, use the **realised yield approach**, which looks into the past. **(5)** All the above calculate the cost of equity **as a balancing figure**; when the **cost of equity or expectation of investors is dependent on risk** — higher the risk, higher the expectation and vice versa — use the **Capital Asset Pricing Model**, which is **based on risk**.

**7.1 Dividend price approach**, also known as the **Dividend Valuation Model**. It **assumes that the dividend per share is expected to remain constant forever**. ==**Ke = D ÷ P0**==, where **D** is the expected dividend (also written as D1) and **P0** the **market price of equity (ex-dividend)**.

**7.2 Earnings price approach.** Its advocates **correlate the earnings of the company with the market price of its share**, so the cost of equity is **based upon the expected rate of earnings of a company**. The argument is that **each investor expects a certain amount of earnings, whether distributed or not**, from the company in whose shares he invests. The study material's illustration: if an investor expects at least a **20% rate of earning** and the company is expected to **earn 30%**, the investor will be prepared to pay **₹150** for each share of ₹100 — that is, (30 ÷ 20) × ₹100.

==**Ke = E ÷ P**, where **E** is current earnings per share and **P** the market price per share.== ==**This approach assumes that the earnings per share will remain constant forever.** The earnings price approach is **similar to the dividend price approach; only it seeks to nullify the effect of changes in the dividend policy**.==
concepts.example: A share trading at ₹80 that is expected to pay a constant dividend of ₹8 has a cost of equity of 10% on the dividend price approach; if EPS is ₹12 and is expected to stay there, the earnings price approach gives 15%.

official_questions.question: Discuss the dividend-price approach to estimating the cost of equity capital.
answer_points: The dividend price approach, also known as the Dividend Valuation Model, makes an assumption that **the dividend per share is expected to remain constant forever**.

The cost of equity capital is computed by **dividing the expected dividend by the market price per share**: **Ke = D ÷ P0**, where D is the expected dividend (also written as D1) and P0 is the market price of equity, ex-dividend.

It is the appropriate method where dividend is expected to be constant; where dividend and earnings are expected to grow at a constant rate, the growth approach or Gordon's model should be used instead.

Cost of equity is the expectation of equity shareholders; because in the case of equity shares the amount of dividend is uncertain — unlike interest or preference dividend, which are fixed — there is no single method of computing it.
official_questions.conclusion: Two marks: the assumption and the formula.

official_questions.question: The capital structure of RSA Limited is as under: equity shares of ₹10 per share ₹1,00,00,000; 8% irredeemable preference shares of ₹100 per share; and other sources as given. Compute the cost of each source of capital and the weighted average cost of capital.
answer_points: **Cost of equity.** ICAI's answer works Ke = D1 ÷ (P0 − F) + g, using the dividend expected next year, the market price less any flotation cost, and the growth rate — in the published solution, Ke = ₹2(1 + 0.05) ÷ (₹60 − ₹4) = **8.75%** on the figures given.
**Cost of irredeemable preference shares (SM §6.1).** Kp = PD ÷ P0, with no tax adjustment, since preference dividend is an appropriation of after-tax profit.
**Cost of debt.** Kd = I(1 − t) ÷ NP for irredeemable debt, or the redeemable formula where a maturity is given, using net proceeds after flotation cost.
**Weighted average cost of capital.** Set out a four-column table — source, amount, weight, cost — and aggregate the products, stating whether book value or market value weights have been used.
The examinable habit here is the table: ICAI's own illustration presents WACC as source, cost of capital, percentage of total capital and product.

expected_questions.question: Explain the five approaches to computing the cost of equity share capital and state when each should be used.
answer_points: Cost of equity is the expectation of equity shareholders. Because the amount of dividend on equity shares is uncertain — unlike interest or preference dividend, which are fixed — there is not a single method but several.
**Dividend price approach:** used if dividend is expected to be constant; Ke = D ÷ P0, where P0 is the market price ex-dividend.

**Earnings price approach:** used if earnings per share is expected to be constant; Ke = E ÷ P. It is similar to the dividend price approach, only it seeks to nullify the effect of changes in dividend policy.
**Growth approach or Gordon's model:** used if dividend and earnings are expected to grow at a constant rate; Ke = D1 ÷ P0 + g.

**Realised yield approach:** used if it is difficult to forecast future dividend or EPS; it looks into the past and treats the average rate of return realised in the past few years as the expected return in future.

**Capital Asset Pricing Model:** used when the cost of equity or expectation of investors is dependent on risk — higher the risk, higher the expectation; Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf). The first four calculate cost of equity as a balancing figure; CAPM is based on risk.

concepts.title: 7.3–7.4 The Growth Approach (Gordon's Model) and the Realised Yield Approach
concepts.evidence: RTP 2 (May 2025, Sep 2024) · MTP 2 (Jan 2025 Series I, Jan 2026 Series II)
understand: **7.3 Growth approach or Gordon's model.** As per this approach, **the rate of dividend growth remains constant**. Where **earnings, dividends and equity share price all grow at the same rate**, ==**Ke = D1 ÷ P0 + g**==, where **D1 = D0(1 + g)**, the next expected dividend, **P0** the current market price per share and **g** the constant growth rate of dividend.

==In the case of **newly issued equity shares where floatation cost is incurred**, the cost of equity with an estimation of constant dividend growth is **Ke = D1 ÷ (P0 − F) + g**, where **F is the flotation cost per share**.==

**Illustration 9.** A company paid a dividend of **₹1 per share** (face value ₹10) last year, expected to grow at **10%** every year, with a market price of **₹55**. Ke = [₹1(1 + 0.1) ÷ ₹55] + 0.10 = **0.12, or 12%**.

**Estimating the growth rate — method (i), the average method.** ==**Current Dividend (D0) = Dn(1 + g)<sup>n</sup>**, so **growth rate = (D0 ÷ Dn)<sup>1/n</sup> − 1**.== Using future value tables: **divide D0 by Dn**, find that result in the corresponding year's row, and **read off the interest rate for the corresponding column** — that is the growth rate. The study material's Example 4: current dividend ₹16.10, dividend 5 years ago ₹10; ₹16.10 ÷ ₹10 = 1.61, found in the 5th year row at the 10% column, so **g = 10%**.

**Estimating the growth rate — method (ii), Gordon's growth model.** ==Unlike the average method, this **attempts to derive a future growth rate**: an **increase in the level of investment will give rise to an increase in future dividends**, so it takes the **earnings retention rate (b)** and the **rate of return on investments (r)** into account: **g = b × r**==, where **b is the proportion of earnings available to equity shareholders which is not distributed as dividend**.

**7.4 Realised yield approach.** ==**The average rate of return realised in the past few years is historically regarded as the 'expected return' in the future.**== It computes cost of equity **based on the past records of dividends actually realised by the equity shareholders**.

**Its unrealistic assumptions**, as the study material lists them: **risks faced by the company remain the same; the shareholders continue to expect the same rate of return; and the reinvestment opportunity cost (rate) of the shareholders is the same as the realised yield**. ==**If the earnings do not remain stable, this method is not practical.**==

**Illustration 10.** Mr. Mehra purchased a share of Alpha Limited for **₹1,000**, received dividend for five years at **10%**, and sold the share at the end of the fifth year for **₹1,128**. The realised rate of return is the discount rate which equates the present value of the five dividends plus the present value of the sale price to the purchase price. That rate is approximately **12%**, and **12% is the cost of equity**.

**Illustration 11 — the geometric mean route.** Where yearly dividends and prices are given, first compute the yield for each year as **(D<sub>t</sub> + P<sub>t</sub>) ÷ P<sub>t−1</sub>**, then take the geometric mean: ==**Ke = [(1 + Y1) × (1 + Y2) × … × (1 + Yn)]<sup>1/n</sup> − 1**==. In the study material's example this gives **[1.1944 × 1.2821 × 1.0609 × 1.0772]<sup>1/4</sup> − 1 = 0.15, or 15%**.
concepts.example: A share at ₹120 expected to pay ₹6 next year with 8% growth costs 6 ÷ 120 + 0.08 = 13%. If ₹4 of flotation cost is incurred on a fresh issue, it costs 6 ÷ 116 + 0.08 = 13.17%.

official_questions.question: P Ltd. has the following capital structure at book value as on 31st March 2024: equity share capital (1,00,000 shares) ₹10,00,000; 12% preference shares ₹15,00,000; 10% debentures ₹15,00,000; total ₹40,00,000. The equity shares are currently traded at ₹100 per share. The company expects to pay a dividend of ₹5 per equity share next year, with dividends projected to grow perpetually at 5% per annum. The corporate tax rate is 35%. Calculate the weighted average cost of capital based on the current capital structure, and recalculate it if the company raises an additional ₹5 lakh of debt by issuing 12% debentures.
answer_points: **Cost of equity (SM §7.3).** Ke = D1 ÷ P0 + g = ₹5 ÷ ₹100 + 0.05 = 0.05 + 0.05 = **0.10, or 10%**. Note that ₹5 is already the dividend expected next year, so no (1 + g) adjustment is needed.
**Cost of preference shares (SM §6.1).** Kp = PD ÷ P0 = 12% with no tax adjustment, preference dividend being an appropriation of after-tax profit.
**Cost of debentures (SM §5.2).** Kd = I(1 − t) ÷ NP = 10% × (1 − 0.35) = **6.5%** for the existing debentures issued at par.

**Recalculated WACC with ₹5 lakh of new 12% debentures.** The new debt costs 12% × (1 − 0.35) = **7.8%**, the total capital becomes ₹45,00,000, and the weights are recalculated before aggregating again.
Recomputing WACC before and after a change in the structure is the commonest MTP format in this chapter — six of the fourteen MTPs ask for it twice.

The realised rate of return is the **discount rate which equates the present value of the dividends received in the past five years plus the present value of the sale price of ₹1,128 to the purchase price of ₹1,000**.

Dividends are ₹100 a year for five years and the sale proceeds ₹1,128 at the end of year 5. At **12%**, the present value of the dividends plus the present value of the sale price is ₹1,000.076, against a purchase price of ₹1,000. **The realised rate of return, and hence the cost of equity, is therefore 12%.**

**Assumptions, which the study material itself calls unrealistic:** the risks faced by the company remain the same; the shareholders continue to expect the same rate of return; and the reinvestment opportunity cost of the shareholders is the same as the realised yield.
If the earnings do not remain stable, this method is not practical.

concepts.title: 7.5 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) Approach
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (Sep 2024 Q2(a), Jan 2025 Q2(a), Jan 2026 Q1(c)) · MTP 2 (May 2026 Series I, Sep 2026 Series II)
understand: ==**CAPM describes the risk-return trade-off for securities; it describes the linear relationship between risk and return of securities.**==

**Two kinds of risk.** **(i) Unsystematic risk**, also called **company specific risk**, as it is related to the company's performance. ==It **can be reduced or eliminated by diversification of the securities portfolio**, and is also known as **diversifiable risk**.== Examples: **a strike or lockdown in the company, labour not available**. **(ii) Systematic risk** is the **macro-economic or market specific risk under which a company operates**. ==It **cannot be eliminated by diversification, hence it is non-diversifiable**.== Examples: **inflation, government policy, interest rate**.

==Since diversifiable risk can be eliminated by the investor through diversification, **a business should be concerned, as per CAPM, solely with non-diversifiable risk**.== The non-diversifiable risks are **assessed in terms of the beta coefficient (β), through fitting a regression equation between the return of a security and the return on a market portfolio**.

==**Cost of Equity (Ke) = Rf + β(Rm − Rf)**==, where **Ke** is the cost of equity capital, **Rf** the risk free rate of return, **β** the beta coefficient, **Rm** the rate of return on the market portfolio and **(Rm − Rf)** the **market risk premium**. So **required rate of return = risk free rate + risk premium**.

**The idea behind CAPM**, as the study material puts it, is that **investors need to be compensated in two ways: (i) time value of money and (ii) risk**. ==The **time value of money is represented by the risk-free rate** in the formula and **compensates investors for placing money in any investment over a period of time**; the **beta term represents the compensation for the additional risk taken**.==

**Reading beta.** A beta of 1 means the security moves with the market; above 1 it is more volatile than the market and the required return is higher; below 1 it is less volatile and the required return lower. The study material presents this as the **risk-return relationship of various securities** on a line rising from the risk-free rate.

**Why the paper likes it.** CAPM is the one cost-of-equity method that needs **no dividend history and no growth estimate** — three inputs and one line of arithmetic — so it can be set as a one-mark MCQ or as the opening line of a seven-mark WACC question.
concepts.example: September 2024: Rf 10%, beta 1.75, market return 12%. Ke = 10% + 1.75 × (12% − 10%) = 13.5% — one line, one mark.

provisions.requirement: Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf); β measures non-diversifiable risk, fitted by regression between the security's return and the market portfolio's return.
provisions.exam_angle: Asked in three of the last six past papers as the first line of the answer.

provisions.requirement: Unsystematic risk is company specific and diversifiable; systematic risk is macro-economic and non-diversifiable; CAPM concerns itself solely with the latter.
provisions.exam_angle: A clean 2-mark theory part and a frequent MCQ.

memory.trick: **Unsystematic is Unique to the company and can be Undone by diversification. Systematic Stays.** CAPM prices only what stays.
key: Compensation for time value of money
Inflation, government policy, interest rate — non-diversifiable

mistakes: Multiplying beta by Rm instead of by the market risk premium (Rm − Rf).
Treating (Rm − Rf) as already given when the question supplies Rm — read carefully which one is stated.
Saying CAPM covers total risk; it covers non-diversifiable risk only.

official_questions.question: CMC Limited: number of equity shares 20,00,000; book value of 10% convertible debentures ₹1,00,00,000; book value of 12% bank term loan ₹25,00,000; market price of equity share ₹55; market value of 10% convertible debenture ₹108; face value of equity share ₹10. Compute (i) the cost of equity share capital by the Capital Asset Pricing Model approach, (ii) the cost of the convertible debenture by the approximation method, (iii) the cost of the bank term loan, and (iv) the weighted average cost of capital using market value weights.
answer_points: **(i) Cost of equity by CAPM (SM §7.5).** Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf). ICAI's published answer uses Rf = 4.5%, Rm − Rf = 9% and β = 1.5, giving Ke = 4.5% + 1.5 × 9% = **18%**.

**(ii) Cost of the convertible debenture (SM §5.4).** First fix the redemption value as the higher of the cash value and the value of the shares on conversion; then Kd = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2], with NP taken as the market value of ₹108.
**(iii) Cost of the bank term loan (SM §5).** The cost of a loan from a financial institution is computed like redeemable debt; with no issue expenses and redemption at par, Kd = 12% × (1 − t).

**(iv) Weighted average cost of capital on market value weights (SM §9.1).** Market value of equity = 20,00,000 shares × ₹55; market value of the convertible debentures = number of debentures × ₹108; the bank term loan is taken at book value. Weight each and aggregate.
The instruction 'using market value weights' governs part (iv): the study material calls market value weights more correct and more representative of a firm's capital structure.
official_questions.conclusion: Three costs and a market-value weighted average; CAPM opens and the weights close.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.

official_questions.question: AB Infra Projects Limited: equity shares (face value ₹10) ₹60,00,000; 12% preference share capital ₹20,00,000; 10% convertible debentures ₹40,00,000; total ₹1,20,00,000. Risk-free rate 6%, equity beta 1.25, equity risk premium 8%. The 12% preference shares of ₹100 each are irredeemable with a flotation cost of 4% and a current market price of ₹100. The 10% convertible debentures of ₹100 each are issued with a stated maturity. Corporate tax 30%. Answer five questions: cost of equity by CAPM and cost of irredeemable preference capital; redemption value of the debenture; cost of the convertible debentures by the approximation method; weighted average cost of capital using market value weights; and the market price per equity share given profit after tax of ₹48,00,000 and a P/E ratio of 21.
answer_points: **Cost of equity by CAPM.** Ke = Rf + β × risk premium = 6% + 1.25 × 8% = **16%**. Note that the question gives the **equity risk premium** directly, so there is no need to deduct Rf from a market return.
**Cost of irredeemable preference capital (SM §6.1).** Kp = PD ÷ P0 where P0 is net of the 4% flotation cost: ₹12 ÷ (₹100 × 0.96) = ₹12 ÷ ₹96 = **12.5%**. No tax adjustment applies.

**Redemption value of the convertible debenture (SM §5.4).** The higher of the cash value of ₹100 and the value of the shares receivable on conversion, compounded at the growth rate over the remaining life.
**Cost of the convertible debentures.** Kd = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP) ÷ n] ÷ [(RV + NP) ÷ 2], with I = ₹10 and t = 30%.
**Weighted average cost of capital on market value weights.** Weight the three sources at market value and aggregate Ke × We + Kp × Wp + Kd × Wd.
**Market price per equity share.** Number of equity shares = ₹60,00,000 ÷ ₹10 = 6,00,000; EPS = ₹48,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = ₹8; MPS = EPS × P/E ratio = ₹8 × 21 = **₹168** (SM Ch 3 §3.4.4).
This was the first time ICAI examined the whole chapter through a five-part case scenario worth 10 marks.
official_questions.conclusion: Five parts, 2 marks each; the last one crosses into the market ratios of Chapter 3.

official_questions.question: Vertex Industries Ltd. is evaluating the cost of equity for its upcoming expansion project. Calculate the cost of equity using CAPM, and compare the cost of equity for two competitor firms, Competitor A (β = 1.2) and Competitor B (β = 0.8).
answer_points: **Formula (SM §7.5):** Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf), where Rf is the risk free rate, β the beta coefficient and (Rm − Rf) the market risk premium.
**Competitor A**, with β = 1.2, is **more volatile than the market**: its required return exceeds the market return, because a beta above 1 means greater exposure to non-diversifiable risk.
**Competitor B**, with β = 0.8, is **less volatile than the market**: its required return falls below the market return.
The difference between the two costs is exactly **(1.2 − 0.8) × (Rm − Rf) = 0.4 × the market risk premium**, which is the clearest way to present the comparison.

The comparison illustrates the study material's point that CAPM describes a **linear relationship between risk and return**, and that a business should be concerned solely with non-diversifiable risk, since diversifiable risk can be eliminated by the investor.
official_questions.conclusion: One formula applied three times; the comparison is the marks.

expected_questions.question: Explain the Capital Asset Pricing Model approach to computing the cost of equity, distinguishing systematic from unsystematic risk.
answer_points: CAPM describes the risk-return trade-off for securities: it describes the linear relationship between the risk and the return of securities.

**Unsystematic risk** is company specific risk, related to the company's own performance — a strike or lockdown, labour not being available. It can be reduced or eliminated by diversification of the securities portfolio, and is therefore also known as diversifiable risk.

**Systematic risk** is the macro-economic or market specific risk under which a company operates — inflation, government policy, interest rate. It cannot be eliminated by diversification and is therefore non-diversifiable.

Since diversifiable risk can be eliminated by the investor, a business should be concerned, as per CAPM, solely with non-diversifiable risk, which is assessed in terms of the beta coefficient through fitting a regression equation between the return of a security and the return on a market portfolio.

**Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf)**, where Rf is the risk free rate of return, β the beta coefficient, Rm the rate of return on the market portfolio and (Rm − Rf) the market risk premium. Investors need to be compensated in two ways — for the time value of money, represented by the risk-free rate, and for risk, represented by the beta term.

concepts.title: 8. Cost of Retained Earnings
understand: ==Like other sources of fund, **retained earnings also involves cost**: it is the **opportunity cost of dividends foregone by shareholders**.== A company can either **keep or reinvest cash, or return it to shareholders as dividends**; ==if the cash is reinvested, **the opportunity cost is the expected rate of return that shareholders could have obtained by investing in financial assets**.==

==**The cost of retained earnings is often used interchangeably with the cost of equity**, as it is nothing but the expected return of the shareholders from their investment in the shares of the company. **However, normally the cost of equity remains higher than the cost of retained earnings, due to issue of shares at a price lower than the current market price and floatation cost.**==
**The formulas are the same as for cost of equity.** **Dividend price method: Kr = D ÷ P.** **Earnings price method: Kr = EPS ÷ P.** **Growth method: Kr = D1 ÷ P0 + g.**

==**The one difference that matters.** For the calculation of **Ke**, P = net proceeds realised, i.e. **issue price less floatation cost**. But for the calculation of **Kr**, P = **current market price** (though sometimes the issue price may also be used). ==**The concept of floatation cost is not used for the calculation of cost of retained earnings.**==

**Illustration 13.** The face value of equity shares is ₹10 and the current market price ₹200. A new project is to be financed **partly by a new issue and partly by retained earnings**, with an **issue price of ₹190** and **floatation cost of ₹5** per share. The dividend at the end of the first year is expected to be ₹10 and the growth rate 5%. **Kr = ₹10 ÷ ₹200 + 0.05 = 10%.** **Ke = ₹10 ÷ (₹190 − ₹5) + 0.05 = 10.41%.** The gap of 0.41 percentage points is exactly the cost of raising fresh money.
**Illustration 15.** Rf = 7%, β = 1.20, Rm − Rf = 6%. **Kr = Rf + β(Rm − Rf) = 7% + 1.20 × 6% = 14.2%** — so CAPM serves for retained earnings too.

official_questions.question: Lavanya Limited wishes to raise additional finance of ₹20 lakh for meeting its investment plans. It has ₹4,20,000 in the form of retained earnings available for investment purposes. The debt/equity mix is 3:7; the cost of debt is 8% before tax up to ₹3,60,000 and 12% before tax beyond that; earnings per share ₹5; dividend payout and other details as given. Determine the pattern for raising the additional finance, the post-tax average cost of additional debt, the cost of retained earnings and cost of equity, and the overall weighted average after-tax cost of additional finance.
answer_points: **(a) Pattern for raising the additional finance.** With a debt/equity mix of 3:7, **equity = 70% of ₹20,00,000 = ₹14,00,000** and **debt = 30% of ₹20,00,000 = ₹6,00,000**. Of the equity portion, ₹4,20,000 comes from retained earnings and the balance from a fresh issue.

**(b) Post-tax average cost of additional debt.** Kd = I(1 − t). The first ₹3,60,000 carries 8% before tax and the remaining ₹2,40,000 carries 12%, so the **average is weighted across the two slabs** before applying (1 − t).

**(c) Cost of retained earnings and cost of equity by the dividend growth model.** Ke or Kr = D1 ÷ P0 + g. The two differ because **Kr uses the current market price while Ke uses net proceeds after flotation cost** (SM §8); the concept of flotation cost is not used for retained earnings.

**(d) Overall weighted average after-tax cost of additional finance.** Set out a table of source, amount, weight and cost, and aggregate the products. Because these are marginal weights — the proportions the firm intends to employ — the book value versus market value question does not arise (SM §10).

expected_questions.question: The face value of equity shares of a company is ₹10, while the current market price is ₹200 per share. The company is going to start a new project, financed partly by a new issue and partly by retained earnings. The issue price will be ₹190 per share and the floatation cost ₹5 per share. Dividend at the end of the first year is expected to be ₹10 and the growth rate 5%. Calculate the cost of equity shares and the cost of retained earnings, and explain why they differ.
answer_points: **Cost of retained earnings.** Kr = D1 ÷ P0 + g = ₹10 ÷ ₹200 + 0.05 = 0.05 + 0.05 = **0.10, or 10%**. The current market price is used, because the concept of floatation cost is not applied to retained earnings.
**Cost of equity.** Ke = D1 ÷ (P0 − F) + g = ₹10 ÷ (₹190 − ₹5) + 0.05 = ₹10 ÷ ₹185 + 0.05 = **0.1041, or 10.41%**. Here P is the net proceeds realised: issue price less floatation cost.

**Why they differ.** Cost of retained earnings is the opportunity cost of dividends foregone by shareholders — the return they could have obtained by investing in financial assets. Cost of equity is the return required on money newly raised, and the company nets less than the market price because shares are issued at a price lower than the current market price and floatation cost is incurred.
So the cost of equity normally remains higher than the cost of retained earnings; here the gap is 0.41 percentage points.

concepts.title: 9–10. Weighted Average Cost of Capital, the Choice of Weights, and Marginal Cost of Capital
concepts.evidence: PYQ 6 (every attempt May 2024 to May 2026) · RTP 6 · MTP 8
understand: **Why a weighted average (§9).** To balance **financial risk, ownership control over the company and cost of capital**, a company usually **does not procure the entire fund from a single source** but makes a mix. Hence the **cost of total capital equals the weighted average of the cost of individual sources**. ==**WACC is also known as the overall cost of capital**; it **weighs the cost of a particular source with its proportion to the total capital**, and is the **weighted average after-tax cost of the individual components of the firm's capital structure**.==

**The four steps.** **Step 1:** calculate the total capital from all sources (long-term debt + preference share capital + equity share capital + retained earnings). **Step 2:** calculate the proportion of each source to the total capital. **Step 3:** multiply each proportion by the respective cost of capital. **Step 4:** aggregate — that is the WACC.

**The study material's own presentation.** Retained earnings 10% × 25% = 2.50%; equity share capital 11% × 10% = 1.10%; preference share capital 9% × 15% = 1.35%; long-term debts 6% × 50% = 3.00%; **total WACC 7.95%**. Present your answer in exactly this four-column shape.

**Why WACC matters.** ==Securities analysts use WACC when valuing and selecting investments; in **discounted cash flow analysis WACC is the discount rate applied to future cash flows** for deriving net present value, and it can be used as a **hurdle rate against which to assess return on investment capital performance**. **The WACC represents the minimum rate of return at which a company produces value for its investors** — a company returning 20% with a WACC of 11% creates about 9%, while a return below WACC means the company is **shedding value**.==

**9.1 Choice of weights.** **Book value (BV)** weights are **operationally easy and convenient**; reserves such as **share premium and retained profits are included in the book value of equity**, in addition to the nominal value of share capital, and **the value of equity will generally not reflect historic asset values or future prospects**. ==**Market value (MV)** weights are **more correct and represent a firm's capital structure**; it is **preferable to use MV weights for the equity**. While using MV, **reserves such as share premium and retained profits are ignored, as they are in effect incorporated into the value of equity**. MV **represents existing conditions and takes into account changing market conditions and current prices**. For debt too, MV is better than BV, **though the difference may not be very significant**.==

==**There is no separate market value for retained earnings.** The market value of equity shares represents **both paid-up equity capital and retained earnings**. But the **cost of equity is not the same as the cost of retained earnings**. Hence, to give market value weights, **the market value of equity shares should be apportioned in the ratio of the book value of paid-up equity capital and the book value of retained earnings**.== The study material's Illustration 16 does exactly this: book value ₹5,00,000 equity and ₹15,00,000 retained earnings, a ratio of 1:3, applied to a market value of ₹25,00,000 to give ₹6,25,000 and ₹18,75,000.

**The study material's five-point BV versus MV comparison.** **Definition** — BV is based on the historical cost of assets and liabilities recorded on the balance sheet; MV on the current market price of equity and debt. **Reflects current conditions** — BV may not accurately reflect current market conditions or true economic value; MV more accurately reflects them. **Stability** — BV is generally more stable as it does not fluctuate with market conditions; MV can be volatile. **Relevance for investors** — BV is less relevant as it does not consider current market perceptions; MV is more relevant. **Ease of calculation** — BV is easier to calculate using financial statements; MV requires market data which can be more complex to gather.

**10. Marginal cost of capital.** ==**The marginal cost of capital may be defined as the cost of raising an additional rupee of capital.**== Since capital is raised in substantial amounts in practice, it is **referred to as the cost incurred in raising new funds (over and above the existing)**. It is **derived when the average cost of capital is calculated using the marginal weights**.

==**The marginal weights represent the proportion of funds the firm intends to employ.** Thus **the problem of choosing between book value weights and market value weights does not arise in the case of marginal cost of capital computation.**== The **intended financing proportion should be applied as weights to the marginal component costs**, and the marginal cost should be calculated **in the composite sense**.

**When average and marginal costs diverge.** ==**When a firm raises funds in a proportional manner and the component's cost remains unchanged, there will be no difference between the average cost of capital and the marginal cost of capital.**== Component costs **may remain constant up to a certain level of funds raised and then start increasing** — the cost of debt may be 7% after tax till ₹10 lakh, 8% between ₹10 lakh and ₹15 lakh, and so on. Similarly, **if the firm has to use external equity when retained profits are not sufficient, the cost of equity will be higher because of floatation costs**. ==**When the component costs start rising, the average cost of capital will rise, and the marginal cost of capital will, however, rise at a faster rate.**==
